bio.en: Kevin Aluwi is the co-founder and former CEO of Gojek, the Indonesian super-app spanning ride-hailing, payments, and deliveries, which grew into one of Southeast Asia's most valuable startups.
bio.zh: 凯文·阿卢维（Kevin Aluwi）是 Gojek 的联合创始人兼前 CEO，Gojek 是印尼的一款超级应用，涵盖出行、支付与配送，已成长为东南亚最具价值的初创公司之一。

summary.en: Kevin recounts Gojek's early resistance from motorcycle-taxi syndicates who physically attacked drivers, and how the company responded by hiring private security rather than abandoning its contractors. He shares the operating philosophy behind building a multi-service super-app in a chaotic market. The episode is a raw look at the physical and strategic risks of scaling in emerging markets.
summary.zh: 凯文讲述了 Gojek 早期遭遇摩托车出租车团伙的抵制——他们曾对司机大打出手，以及公司如何通过雇佣私人安保、而非抛弃外包司机来应对。他分享了在混乱市场中构建多业务超级应用的运营理念。本期真实呈现了在新兴市场扩张时所面临的体力与战略风险。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: In the early days of Gojek, there was a lot of resistance to our services. The most common form of that resistance in the early days was actually by motorcycle taxi mafia. So you would have these areas that are essentially controlled through violence by specific area mafia. And when we start having drivers pick up orders and pick up passengers, these people would actually physically assault our drivers. We've had everything from bricks thrown at our drivers to knives and machetes being brandished at them, and I think it would've been easy for us to say like, "Hey, they're all contractors. They're third parties, let them kind of just sort it out." But instead, we actually hired private security. So we actually work with private security companies to help our drivers in those situations, to help kind of extract them out of these sticky situations. And so we actually ran a fairly big private security operation for a fairly long time.
turns.zh: 在Gojek成立初期，我们的服务遭遇了诸多阻力。早期最常见的抵制形式来自摩托车出租车黑帮。这些地区实际上被特定地盘的黑帮通过暴力手段控制。当我们的司机开始接单、接送乘客时，这些人就会对司机实施人身攻击。从向司机投掷砖块，到持刀挥舞砍刀相威胁，各种暴力行为层出不穷。面对这种局面，我们本可以轻易采取放任态度——"反正他们都是合同工，是第三方，让他们自己解决吧"。但我们选择了另一种做法：聘请私人安保公司为司机提供援助，帮助他们摆脱险境。为此，我们曾长期运营着一支规模相当大的私人安保队伍。

It's really popular in VC-consultant-analyst circles because it sounds really great on a strategy deck because all of the things that are really appealing, we'll talk about lower customer acquisition costs, higher attach rates to different products, talk about higher retention across different services, the ease of cross-selling and upselling. And one probably really good example that I like to reference is that I remember one of our products was mobile phone top up and recharge. In Southeast Asia, a majority of people are on prepaid plans instead of postpaid plans. So everyone basically buys their minutes and their data plans upfront in the beginning of the week or the beginning of the month. (00:11:27): So we had a product which was a mobile top-up product. And so the reason I mentioned this specific product as a really illustrative point on super apps is that it's a product that 95% plus of our customers need because they're all on prepaid plans. So it's a very relevant product. And we had our UX research research team actually look into why the engagement in the product wasn't as high as we thought it should be. So one of the questions that our URX team asked our customers was like, "Hey, do you know that you could top up your mobile minutes and by data on the Gojek app?" And only about 40% of our customers, like 30 or 40% of our customers knew that this product existed. And that completely blew our minds because one, it's a product that is relevant for all of our customers. (00:12:25): Two, it was literally there on one of the six buttons on the homepage. And I think the insight that we got here was that there kind of needs to be a unifying concept across all of your services within the app for your users to be able to think about your product in a sensible way. And for us, the way that our customers thought about us was that they thought about the driver. And so when we went from ride hailing to package delivery to food delivery, to grocery delivery, customers really understood that. And we didn't have to sell this idea to our customers that you had all of these services under one app because they thought about the Gojek driver. That made sense. You can easily cross sell somebody from a ride hailing customer to a grocery customer or a food delivery customer because they understood the unifying factor there being the driver. (00:13:24): But then when you start doing other things that don't have that unifying factor in terms of the concept that a customer has when they think about your service, it starts breaking down. So one other fun UXR insight here was when we launched massage services. So we had at one point though we've shut it down a few years after, we had massage services where you can order a masseuse to come to your place. And a question that many of our customers asked was that, "oh, is the driver going to come into my house and give me a massage?" And for us, that was insane. Of course not, our drivers are not trained masseuses, but that was the question that people asked because they thought like, "oh, this app is an app for these driver related services, so if there was a massage service, I'm assuming it's that same man who's going to give me a massage." (00:14:17): And so I think this kind of illustrates the importance of having these unifying concepts that are easy for customers to think about the multiple different services. It's not as simple as just saying, oh, we have a lot of engagement, we have a lot of eyeballs at a service. And then you have a super app that makes sense for customers. And so that whole nirvana of lower CAC, higher retention that are all on these great strategy decks often don't pan out because you kind of have to then resell this idea of like, oh, this is another service and that you can use. And that's a bit of investment that you have to actually put in terms of advertising and customer education that increases those customer acquisition costs. (00:15:03): And it also leads to design constraints because there's only so many ways you can display a whole bunch of different services that actually have little to do with each other, which is why when you see super apps today, it's kind of like this giant menu or this giant grid which does limit the design decisions that you can make, which is unfortunate because if you actually, I think it's an unsolved problem at this point.
turns.zh:
好吧，我可能说得有点直接了，但我对最近这个话题被频繁提及确实有点不满。在风投顾问和分析师圈子里，这个概念很火，因为它在战略演示文稿里听起来很棒——比如降低客户获取成本、提高不同产品用户的留存率、促进交叉销售和追加销售。这些听起来确实不错，但现实中很多好处都难以兑现。有一个很典型的例子：我们曾推出过一个移动充值产品。在东南亚，大多数用户使用预付费套餐而非后付费套餐，所以用户通常会在周初或月初预先购买通话分钟和数据套餐。（00:11:27）我们推出了这个移动充值产品，但用户参与度远低于预期。用户研究团队询问："你们知道可以在Gojek应用上充值话费和购买数据套餐吗？"结果只有约40%的用户知道这个功能。这完全出乎我们的意料——毕竟这个产品对95%以上的用户都适用！（00:12:25）更令人惊讶的是，这个产品明明放在首页六个按钮中的一个位置。研究团队发现，要让用户正确理解产品定位，必须在应用内建立统一的服务理念。比如用户原本只把Gojek和司机关联起来，所以当我们从网约车扩展到快递、外卖、生鲜时，用户能顺理成章地接受这些延伸服务。而推广"一站式应用"的概念反而适得其反，因为用户对服务的认知仍局限于司机形象。（00:13:24）还有个案例：我们曾推出按摩服务，但几年后关停了这个业务。用户疑惑："司机会进我家给我按摩吗？"这完全超出了我们的预期——司机根本不是专业按摩师，但用户误以为"这个应用就是司机相关服务的集合体”，导致服务推广失败。
不同的服务。问题并非简单地说一句“我们的服务用户参与度很高，吸引了大量流量”，然后就推出一个对用户有吸引力的超级应用程序。那些声称能降低客户获取成本、提高用户留存率的完美战略方案往往难以落地，因为你必须重新向用户推销这些服务，告诉他们这些服务是可以相互补充的。而这需要投入大量资金用于广告宣传和用户教育，进而推高客户获取成本。  
（00:15:03）此外，这还会带来设计上的限制——毕竟要把一堆彼此关联性不强的不同服务展示出来，方式实在有限。如今我们看到的超级应用程序，往往就是一个巨大的菜单或网格界面，这无疑限制了设计的灵活性。令人遗憾的是，目前这仍是一个尚未解决的难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's hilarious story about the massage product. Sounds like a lot of startups are going to have some issues scaling to new products and trying to become a super app. I want to shift a little bit and talk about brand. I did a little research on you ahead of this chat. I watched your Marshall graduation and speech and a few other interviews you did, and something that came out of your previous writing and talks is just how much you care about brand and how much value you put into brand. And that you just have a lot of opinions about the importance of brand. And to me and to most people, brand is this really squishy thing and it's hard to know what exactly to do to build your brand, when to prioritize it, how to prioritize it amongst other things you're doing, especially early on. So I'd love to hear your advice for founders that are listening and just like, what should I actually do around brand? What's your advice for how to tactically do something about brand and also just why do you think it's so important?
turns.zh: 关于那个按摩产品的故事真是太搞笑了。看来很多初创公司在向新产品扩展规模、试图打造超级应用方面都会遇到不少挑战。我想稍微转换一下话题，聊聊品牌问题。之前在这次对话前，我对您做了一点研究。我看了您在马歇尔学院的毕业典礼致辞，还有您接受的其他几次采访。从您之前的文章和演讲中可以看出，您对品牌的重视程度极高，也对品牌的重要性有很多独到见解。在我和大多数人看来，品牌是个很抽象的概念，很难明确该如何打造品牌、何时将其置于优先地位，以及如何在其他事务中平衡品牌建设，尤其是在初期阶段。所以我很想听听您对听众创业者的建议：在品牌建设方面，具体该怎么做？您有什么实操性的建议？又为什么您认为品牌如此重要？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: I do agree with you that it is kind of this squishy thing that most people see as an afterthought, may be because it is kind of this squishy thing that it's hard to define, but I'm a very big believer that the two most important things in a consumer business are product and brand in that order. And I don't think I need to sell the idea, especially to your audience. That product is absolutely critical and probably the most important. But brand as an afterthought is definitely one of the areas where I think there's a giant missed opportunity for consumer tech businesses. And I get why we opened the session by talking about the size of the business to get an appreciation of the scale for audience members who might be unfamiliar with us or with the region. (00:17:16): But I wish I did have to start there because we actually started as a very scrappy company where we were by far the underfunded player and without brand. We probably would've never gotten to escape velocity beyond that scrappy stage, we've maintained our leadership in Indonesia through a lot of the things that we actually did on the brand side to give you a sense of how scrappy we had to be in competition. (00:17:52): For the first six months after launching our app, we had only raised about $2 million and our regional competitor had already raised 250. So they had literally more than a hundred times more capital than we have. So it's easy to talk about what we built as this kind of giant business, but we came from a place where we were seriously underfunded. And I think a big reason why we survived was that we built a great brand for our consumers and for our drivers and for our merchants. And I think that great brands create associations in their customer's minds that transcend the typically transactional or utilitarian one that most people have with businesses and they become part of one's identity. (00:18:42): I think some of the best-in-class examples of these are probably all the Apple fanboys and fangirls, Nike sneakerheads, for these individuals, the brand becomes a really big part of their identity and their loyalty towards the products of the company go beyond a relationship that can easily be swayed just through discounts or other more features that other competitors might have. And so I'm a really firm believer of how important this is because you can see it if you step out of the tech bubble for a second, you can see that there's so many great companies out there that really rely on the strength of their brand to build these fantastic businesses and to create great experiences for their customers. And you ask, what are the things that one can do? (00:19:45): I think for us, we invested a lot in our brand across multiple areas. And I think one specific area that I think is really important is that you create consistency across all customer touchpoints. And so branding is not just cool logo, cool advertising, fun imagery, but it's really about the impression that a customer or user has with your product and with your business. So having that consistency across all customer touchpoints is really important. So how you write copy and advertising and in the app, how you've even designed the app, but we were the first company of scale to have ads that don't take ourselves too seriously. We make fun of ourselves, we make fun of our cultural observations of Indonesia. And again, to just build this overall field that like, Hey, we get, we are part of the overall culture of Indonesia. And I think even going beyond the more aesthetic or communication oriented investments, we also leaned into cultural artifacts in our product features to really build this brand that is part of day-to-day culture. (00:21:09): One of my favorite cultural artifacts is that in Asia it's fairly common to send food as gifts to your loved ones or maybe people you're interested in dating. So people would send over food as gifts to their romantic interests. And so when we launched our food delivery service, a lot of people were actually using it for this, I'm going to send it to my boyfriend or my girlfriend or the person that I'm interested in dating. And so it became this whole cultural phenomenon of sending go-food for these people and we kind of lean into it in our product feature where all of the other players in the market at the time basically only allowed you to deliver food to your home or your office, but we actually created a feature that allowed you to choose a delivery point that was far away from where you were. (00:22:04): There was a lot of reasons why other companies didn't allow it at the time because it's like, oh, it might be used for fraud and stuff like that. But we leaned into it, we leaned into it and actually created features that allowed to put your pickup point far away from where your actual location was. And then we just had fun with this whole idea of go-food dating. And so yes, it's kind of part of branding, but thinking about branding beyond just marketing communication but actually be as being relatable and being part of the culture and being sensitive of what that culture is, I think was something that we did really well in the early days that allowed us to continue maintaining leadership in spite of the fact that our competitors had more money, which meant that they could offer more discounts, they could offer more incentives to drivers, but we really kind of lean very hard into being not just a utilitarian commodity, which is what a lot of people would say is the nature of our business to some level of accuracy.
turns.zh:
我确实同意你的观点，即大多数人认为品牌是事后才考虑的次要因素，或许正因为它难以定义才被忽视。但我坚信，消费者业务中最重要的两件事是产品和品牌——按此顺序排列。我想无需向你们强调这一点，但尤其对你们的听众而言，我想强调产品至关重要，可能是最关键的因素。而将品牌视为事后之举，绝对是消费科技企业错失良机的一个领域。（00:17:16）但我真希望我们不必从规模谈起，因为我们最初是一家资金严重不足、缺乏品牌认知的初创公司。若没有品牌力量，我们很可能永远无法突破生存瓶颈。我们在印尼保持领先地位的关键，在于我们在品牌建设方面下了大量功夫，这也让你们看到了我们在竞争中必须展现的韧性。（00:17:52）应用上线后的头六个月，我们仅筹集了约200万美元资金，而地区竞争对手已融资2.5亿美元。资金差距达百倍有余。人们很容易将我们打造的巨头视为理所当然，但我们曾深陷资金短缺的困境。能在竞争中存活下来的关键在于，我们为消费者、司机和商家打造了卓越的品牌。优秀的品牌能在客户心智中建立超越传统交易或功利性关系的情感纽带，成为身份认同的一部分。（00:18:42）这方面的典范案例当属苹果粉丝群体、耐克球鞋爱好者。对这些群体而言，品牌已融入他们的身份认同，用户对产品的忠诚度远超折扣或竞品功能的诱惑。因此我坚信品牌至关重要。若跳出科技泡沫思考，就会发现许多伟大公司正是依托品牌力量打造卓越业务、创造非凡体验的。有人会问，企业该如何行动？（00:19:45）对我们而言，我们在多个维度深耕品牌建设。其中最关键的是在所有客户接触点保持品牌一致性。品牌不只是酷炫的标识、广告或趣味图像，更是客户对产品和企业的整体印象。因此在所有客户接触点保持品牌统一至关重要。无论是文案创作、广告投放，还是应用设计，我们都是首家以自嘲姿态投放广告的规模化公司。我们调侃自身、调侃对印尼文化的观察，致力于构建整体品牌语境：我们深谙印尼文化，融入其中。我们甚至超越了美学或传播层面的投资，
我们还在产品功能中融入了文化元素，真正打造出一个深入日常文化的品牌。（00:21:09）：我最喜欢的文化现象之一是，在亚洲，送食物作为礼物给亲人或心仪对象相当常见。比如人们会把食物当作礼物送给心仪的对象。于是当我们推出外卖服务时，很多人都用它来传递情感信号——“我要把这份美食送给男友/女友/心仪的人”。这逐渐演化成一种文化现象——“外卖送礼”风靡一时。当时市场上的其他平台基本只支持将食物送到用户家中或办公室，但我们创新推出了“选择远程取餐点”的功能。

（00:22:04）：其他平台不支持这项功能的原因有很多，比如担心被用于欺诈。但我们坚持创新，打造了允许用户选择远程取餐点的功能，并巧妙地将“外卖送礼”融入产品体验。这种创意不仅是品牌建设，更是深层文化共鸣的体现。我们早期就深刻领悟到，品牌不应局限于营销传播，而是要与用户产生情感共鸣，成为文化的一部分。正因如此，尽管竞争对手资金雄厚、能提供更多折扣和司机激励，我们仍能保持领先地位，因为我们拒绝做冷冰冰的工具型产品——这正是许多人对我们行业的刻板印象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to get even more concrete, one takeaway from what you just shared, which is interesting, is the first part of figuring out how to approach your brand is what's the personality of your product for you? You said it was like we're just of the people, we're like you, we're here to help you, make your life easier. And then that informs the copy, the messaging, be a little, I forget how you describe it, but just almost bad grammar and stuff just because it relates more to people and then some of these product launches that connect to that. So maybe if there's anything else you want to add there that'd be interesting. And then what's like, I don't know, one or two moments that most helped build the brand. I know you're kind of famous for having helmets and jackets on the drivers that help spread the Gojek brand. Is there anything else that just like, wow, this was really effective to build this brand that ended up dominating Indonesia?
turns.zh: 嗯，再具体一点，你刚才分享的观点很有意思。首先，要理解如何打造品牌，关键在于明确产品的人格特质。你说我们的产品就像普通人，能帮助用户让生活更轻松。这为文案和信息传递提供了灵感，甚至可以用一些看似语法不通的表达，只要能更贴近用户心声。比如Gojek的头盔和夹克推广活动，就通过让司机们身着印有品牌标识的装备，在拥堵的城市中穿行，让用户产生联想。还有其他成功案例吗？比如你们如何在印尼市场占据主导地位？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: The jackets and helmets piece I think is really, really important for two reasons. One, the more obvious reason, which is that because they were just all over the streets of many cities in Indonesia, people were familiar with the imagery and the names, but I think it's also really important that people saw what was happening. So if we were like, I don't know, an airline and we branded a bunch of people on the streets with our brand, yeah, sure, that might help with brand recall and people might know about the name. But what was really powerful was that when people would be seeing these drivers with their jackets and helmets, they would be seeing passengers on the backseat as they were stuck in traffic. So I'm stuck in traffic and I'm seeing these people whiz past me with with this imagery on them, and immediately I get that association like, oh, I'm stuck in traffic, but I could be out there cutting through traffic on a motorcycle or you see them carrying packages or delivering food, and you immediately get like, oh, these are guys who can deliver food or deliver packages for me. (00:25:14): And so it was like this beautiful combination of one just having that imagery and having that visual everywhere as a reminder of the brand. But more importantly, it was also a physical reminder of the service of what we do and of how we can help you. And so looking for these opportunities where again, customers can make that connection between the logo and the colors and the name with actually what the service is, I think are the opportunities that I would say people should look out for. They're admittedly quite rare, which is why in my opinion, the laziest kind of branding tends to be the most popular. Just put your name and your copy on a billboard or on a CPM or CPC campaign. But there are these opportunities I think, on being able to reinforce the value proposition of your business in a way that is beyond just visual recall. And I think that was why that specific anecdote is something I like to talk about because it was really one of those special things that reminded people on why we're here.
turns.zh: 头盔和夹克推广活动确实非常重要，原因有两个。首先，最明显的是这些装备在印尼多个城市随处可见，人们对品牌形象和名称都耳熟能详。但更重要的是，人们看到这些身着品牌装备的司机时，往往会联想到自己被困在车流中的场景。被堵在路上的人看到这些司机身着印有品牌标识的装备，瞬间会产生联想：哦，我被堵在这里了，但我本可以骑摩托车穿行于车流中；或者看到他们背着包裹、送餐，立刻会想：哦，这些人能为我送餐、送货。这种将品牌视觉与实际服务相结合的绝妙方式，才是值得关注的关键。当然，这样的机会确实难得，这也是为什么在我看来，最简单粗暴的品牌推广方式往往最受欢迎。比如在广告牌或CPM、CPC广告上堆砌品牌名称和宣传语。但像Gojek这样的案例，才是真正能强化品牌价值主张的典范。这也是我特别喜欢分享这个故事的原因，它确实是能让人们记住我们存在意义的特殊案例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think you tweeted that it was one of the most important things you ever did as a company is decide to put these logos on the helmets and jackets. Reminds me of Lyft's pink mustache, which went away, but felt like a really important way for them to differentiate.
turns.zh: 是啊，我记得你发过推文，说在公司历史上，决定把品牌标识印在头盔和夹克上是最重要的决策之一。这让我想起Lyft的粉色胡子宣传，虽然后来取消了，但确实是他们差异化品牌的有效方式。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: No, totally.
turns.zh: 没错，完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about how scrappy you've been, and I want to dig into that a little bit more. I think there's like US startup scrappy, and then there's like Gojek scrappy, and it'd be fun to hear maybe a story or two just to illustrate how ridiculously scrappy you were as a company early on, especially.
turns.zh: 你之前提到过自己有多么富有拼劲，我想再深入探讨一下这个话题。我觉得有两种拼劲：一种是美国初创企业的拼劲，另一种是 Gojek 这样的公司所展现的拼劲。如果你能分享一两个故事，来说明你们公司早期阶段是多么令人惊叹的拼劲，那就太棒了。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: One thing that we did in the early days that was absolutely crazy was that we were one of the pioneering companies, one of the pioneering technology companies in Indonesia and in Southeast Asia. And so we came into a environment where a lot of the things that maybe companies or people in more developed economies take for granted, for example, having electronic or digital payments, that was something that actually didn't really exist that much when we first started. And so we had a problem of actually trying to pay drivers because drivers every day we would be paying out incentives or just having customers pay with their credit cards or their store balance, and then we'd have a challenge and getting our drivers to actually be able to take that money out for their earnings. And in the early days, we actually had cash booths. So we actually had physical spaces with a vault and cash sitting in the vault where drivers can show up that, oh, this is my driver ID and this is the balance that I have with you. Please give me the cash. (00:28:31): And so we would have these actual physical locations where there would be lions of drivers essentially taking cash. And we eventually figured this out of like, okay, we'll work with a bank and integrate with an ATM network and all that. But in the early days we just did it ourselves of building essentially a mini at ATM network, which I think even that sounds too fancy of what it was it. Because it was literally a booth with a vault with cash in it. And we had at the time already tens of thousands of drivers all across in Indonesia. (00:29:10): Another scrappy story that actually Crystal reminded me of recently that we did was at the time there was a lot of fake driver apps out there because we didn't have all of the security investments that we eventually made, things like code obfuscation and better API security that wouldn't allow for these fraudulent driver apps, these basically third party driver apps to connect to our platform. So there were a lot of these drivers using these third party driver apps that were doing things that... So they were kind of doing unsavory things like stealing driver details, some of them even as bad as financial details so that they can then at some point drain driver funds. And the way that they did it, the way that they convinced drivers to actually use these apps was that they actually added some features that at the time we didn't allow. So things like we wanted drivers to be conscious of what was happening on the app, and so we would actually make sure that drivers would push the accept order button. (00:30:28): We made sure that that was the only way that drivers could accept orders, but this app had a functionality that would automatically accept orders as soon as they came in. And so actually it was kind of this interesting situation where they were doing things that were fraudulent and were not safe for the integrity of the platform, but at the same time they were also providing some value to the people who were using them. And so at the time we had to make a decision of like, okay, we need to nip this in the bud and one way that we could have done it, that would've taken time was it really invest in a lot of the technical security aspects of it, but we didn't have the bandwidth to be able to do that. Engineering and security talent is actually super scarce in Southeast Asia at the time, still is today, but at that time extremely scarce. (00:31:25): And so we ended up making the decision of actually copying those features. So we actually saw all of these third party fraudulent apps and instead of building a whole system to prevent them from being built or preventing them from working on the platform, we just said, "Hey, let's take their top two or three features and let's build them into our app." And that actually significantly reduced the number of users on these third party apps just by having this mentality of you can't beat them, then join them. And that I would say that wasn't a philosophical decision or a principal decision. Is was actually a decision made out of necessity because we simply couldn't build all the capability to combat these apps at the time?
turns.zh:
早期阶段，我们做过一些近乎疯狂的尝试。作为印尼及东南亚地区首批科技创新型公司之一，我们面临着许多发达经济体中被视为理所当然的挑战，比如电子支付与数字支付等基础设施。在刚起步时，印尼的移动支付生态几乎一片空白。司机们每天只能通过现金激励、客户信用卡支付或平台余额来获取报酬，但如何让司机提取这笔收入却成了难题。最初，我们甚至开设了现金兑付亭——一个设有保险箱的实体场所，司机们需出示身份证件并核对余额后，方可领取现金。（00:28:31）

随着业务发展，团队逐渐与银行合作接入ATM网络，但早期我们自主搭建了迷你ATM网络，简单说就是一个设有保险箱的兑付亭。当时我们已在印尼拥有数万名司机用户。（00:29:10）

另一则创业故事是关于打击虚假司机应用的。由于缺乏代码混淆、API安全等防护措施，第三方应用能轻易接入平台。这些应用通过添加违规功能，如自动接单按钮等，诱骗司机使用，最终窃取账户信息甚至资金。（00:30:28）

面对这种安全困境，我们选择复制竞争对手的功能，强制要求司机通过专用按钮接单，同时封禁自动接单功能。这既保护了平台数据，也为用户提供了便利。（00:31:25）
面对第三方应用的欺诈行为，我们没有去构建一套完整的系统来阻止它们被开发或在平台上运行，而是选择了另一种策略：将这些应用的两到三个核心功能整合到我们的应用中。这实际上有效地减少了使用这些第三方应用的用户数量，因为我们秉持了"无法击败对手，那就加入他们"的理念。我认为这并非出于理念或原则上的考量，而是迫于无奈的选择——因为当时我们根本没有能力全面打击这些应用。

turns.zh: 您是正在招聘，还是在寻求新的职业机会呢？无论哪种情况，都请访问 lennysjobs.com/talent 看看吧。若您是招聘经理，可以注册并获取数百名精心筛选的求职者的信息，这些人正积极寻找新的机遇。已有数千人申请加入这个人才库，而我个人只会筛选并接纳约10%的申请者。您在这里能找到最优质的产品经理和增长团队成员，目前已有近百家公司通过这个平台积极招聘。（00:32:44）若您正在主动或被动寻找新的机会，加入这个人才库完全免费。您可以保持匿名，甚至可以选择不向特定公司公开信息。您也可以随时退出，只会收到您感兴趣的公司发来的消息。请访问 lennysjobs.com/talent 了解详情。（00:33:03）您提到的那些趣事真是令人捧腹——不得不与那些山寨破解版应用、欺诈应用竞争，还要在全国范围内搭建现金收付网络。太不可思议了！我就知道这个问题会有精彩的故事，果然没让我失望。Gojek内部那种迎难而上的精神也让人印象深刻，您分享的几个故事对比那些简单粗暴的策略……很多初创公司都奉行"走捷径"，但你们似乎更倾向于迎难而上。为什么会这样？这种精神从何而来？还有其他类似的决策案例吗？比如，你们是如何坚持走难路线的？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: I really don't like the idea of moats. Again, one of the concepts that gets thrown out a lot by strategy type folks of what's the moat of your business or your product? And usually people are looking for an answer like, oh, look at this capability or look at this feature or look at this distribution partner or all of those kind of things. And I don't believe that any moats are durable over time. Eventually with enough time all moats can be crossed. And I think one so-called moat that doesn't get talked about enough is the fact that you're able to do hard things because hard things are hard and just simply doing things that are hard, as long as they create value to your customers, actually is a position that makes it harder for your competitors to be able to win over your customers because it's hard to do those things. (00:34:52): And probably another example of doing something that sounds very difficult was that in the early days of Gojek, there was a lot of resistance to our services and one of the forms of that resistance, one of the more most common form of that resistance in the early days was actually by motorcycle taxi mafia. So you would have these areas that are essentially controlled through violence by specific area mafia. And when we start having drivers pick up orders and pick up passengers, these people would actually physically assault our drivers. We've had everything from bricks thrown at our drivers to knives and machetes being brandished at them to just physical altercations, literally mobs of people getting into these brawls. And there was a lot of these kind of things that actually happened in the streets of Jakarta at the time. And I think it would've been easy for us to say, "Hey, they're all contractors, they're third parties, let them kind of just sort it out." (00:36:14): But instead we actually hired private security. So we actually work with private security companies to help these situations, to help our drivers in those situations, to help extract them out of these sticky situations. And so we actually ran a fairly big private security operation for a fairly long time until it became common to have Gojek drivers do all of these things across cities. We actually ran this very operation intensive thing just to make sure that our drivers could be as safe as possible and it showed our commitment to the driver community, it showed our commitment that we cared. And again, going back to that earlier point around having that branding association, drivers knew that, hey, we weren't just a platform that didn't care. We actually cared about their safety and that helped build that goodwill even as competitors started coming in and paying more money, we still had a lot of loyalty within the driver community because of things like that.
turns.zh: 我真的不喜欢护城河这个概念。再说一次，战略派们总爱抛出这个问题：你公司的护城河是什么？或者你的产品护城河是什么？通常人们会给出诸如“看看这个功能”、“看看这个分销伙伴”之类的答案。但我认为，没有任何护城河能经受住时间的考验。最终，随着时间推移，所有护城河都会被跨越。我认为一个被忽视的所谓护城河是——你能做难事。这类事本身就很难，只要能为客户创造价值，单纯做难事就能让竞争对手更难赢得客户，因为这些事很难做到。（00:34:52）：再举个听起来很困难的例子。在Gojek成立初期，我们的服务遭遇了大量抵制。早期最常见的抵制形式之一来自摩托车出租车黑帮。雅加达街头有一些区域，基本被暴力控制的黑帮把持。当我们让司机接单和接客时，这些人会对司机进行人身攻击。手段从向司机扔砖头、挥舞刀具和砍刀，到大规模斗殴，无所不有。我们当时在雅加达街头经历了太多此类事件。若我们轻易说"他们都是承包商，是第三方，让他们自己解决"，那就太简单了。（00:36:14）：但我们实际雇佣了私人安保公司。通过与这些公司合作，我们帮助司机摆脱困境，化解危机。为了确保司机安全，我们运营了规模庞大的安保体系。直到Gojek司机在各城市都能熟练应对此类情况，我们才停止这项高强度工作。这种高投入的安保模式让司机感受到我们的关怀。即使竞争对手开出更高薪资，我们的司机群体依然忠诚，这源于我们对安全的重视。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did you actually have a security person on a motorcycle? Were they pretending to be the rider and then just get out and punch them in the face?
turns.zh: 你们怎么能让安保人员骑摩托车呢？他们是假扮成骑手，然后突然跳出来打人吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: A minority of situations were like that, but a lot of that was just like, having an on-call service where they could just dial a number and somebody within a 5-10 minute distance would actually show up. And so we would have these patrols effectively in specific hotspots where if there was a situation brewing that they would instantly or almost instantly show up to the site and help diffuse it.
turns.zh: 少数情况是这样，但更多的是按需服务模式。司机拨打求助电话后，5-10分钟内就能有安保人员赶到现场。这些巡逻队会针对高风险区域，一旦出现冲突，几乎能即刻赶到现场化解危机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you have this super app that's doing all these things for people. Plus within the company you've built all these mini businesses, like a whole bank to pay people, private security company. There's probably some other... Crystal shared a story of you guys rented out a stadium for drivers to collect all the drivers and give them phones.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你们开发了这款超级应用，为人们提供了诸多便利。更重要的是，在公司内部，你们还打造了多个微型业务，比如专门的支付银行、私人安保公司之类的。可能还有其他的……Crystal分享了一个故事，说你们曾租下一个体育场，让司机们把所有员工召集起来，给他们分发手机。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. This is great.
turns.zh: 好吧。这真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yeah, that I think is probably one of the hallmarks of this region in general where I have no doubt that what we were building and what we are today is a technology company, but I do think that in the early days you do have to be a lot more operations heavy. And then I think that lends to that scrappiness because there are a lot of things that to solve elegantly and technically will take a lot of time and just kind of over focusing on those type of solutions I think would be doing your customers a disservice because there are opportunities to make things a lot better just through probably more innovation in operations to kind of kickstart things until you have the more elegant, scalable, technical or product solution.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这或许是这个地区的典型特质之一。我毫不怀疑，我们过去创建的公司，以及如今的业务，确实是一家科技公司，但我认为在早期阶段，运营层面的投入确实更多。这种灵活应变的精神也由此而来——因为很多问题若想通过精妙的技术方案解决，往往需要耗费大量时间。但如果过度专注于这类解决方案，我觉得对用户来说未必是好事，因为其实有很多机会通过在运营层面进行创新来显著提升用户体验，进而推动业务发展，最终再打造出更优雅、更具可扩展性的技术或产品解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me that at Gojek, you held tons of different roles throughout the time you were there. You were obviously co-founder, your Co-CEO at one point, defacto CPO at one point, CIO, CFO. I heard that you were writing like push notification copy, became a driver at one point just to keep things running. So feels like another good example of exactly what you're talking about of just doing the hard thing in the operational component.
turns.zh: 这让我想起在Gojek任职期间，你承担过各种各样的角色。你显然是联合创始人，还曾担任过联席CEO，实际上还兼任过首席产品官、首席信息官和首席财务官。据说你还亲自撰写过推送通知的文案，甚至曾化身司机来维持业务运转。所以这似乎又是一个典型的例子，充分诠释了你在运营层面勇于直面挑战的精神。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: I mean, yes, actually I did have a stint as an amateur performance marketer in the early days of Gojek. I would write copy, I would upload ads onto Facebook and Google and try and do my best in optimizing our online marketing spend. But I think I did all of those things, not because I wanted to be scrappy necessarily, but I do think that as, and this is probably most relevant for founders, less for executives, but I think as a founder, I do think it's really important to understand the work that needs to be done in order to see what excellence looks like. And for us, again, we came from an ecosystem where the availability of experienced talent was relatively low. And so for me it was very hard to be able to say, "oh, let's hire person X from organization Y with job description Z," and we know that they probably can deliver because again, the talent availability was really low. (00:41:16): And so a lot of times I felt like I needed to understand, okay, what is this job? What exactly does it entail is, and seeing how bad I am at it allowed me to understand what good looked like. And so I held a lot of those roles just because I wanted to understand every part of the business as best as I could in order to then find somebody who could do it orders of magnitude better than myself. I would say that is true for all of these roles except for being a driver. I think being a driver, I wasn't trying to understand what excellence as a driver look like. Obviously the drivers do a really challenging job and I think I just wanted to understand what that role was like to build a lot more empathy towards the job and make sure that our product was catered towards what those needs were. (00:42:12): So when we first launched our car ride hailing services, I think I was the first actual driver on the app and I would every now and then be a driver. And I remember the early days when I actually picked up a customer. It was this lady and she put in her destination as a mall. And so I went to this house and I knew that, okay, I needed to drive to this mall, but then this lady comes out with this giant bag and so I had to hop out the car, take this giant bag, put it in my trunk, and then off we went. And in the middle of the drive she's like, "Hey, I need to drop off and do my laundry on the way to the mall." And I just had to, "okay, cool." We took a detour, I lugged this giant bag out of our trunk and helped this lady do her laundry. (00:43:17): And then we went to the mall and I got very little money out of that experience and it wasn't instant, but this is eventually what led to, I think a lot of the support I gave to our driver teams when they were pushing for, Hey, we need more waiting fees, we need to add multiple stops in order to make sure that hey, a lot of this extra work was actually compensated. And it was something that I obviously experienced personally and it was something that I definitely was excited about as a set of product features and principles when it came to building our driver app.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，是的，实际上我在Gojek初期确实做过一段时间的业余营销推广工作。我会写文案，在Facebook和谷歌上投放广告，尽力优化我们的在线营销支出。但我觉得我做这些事情，不是因为我必须得精打细算，而是因为——这对创始人来说可能更相关，对高管则没那么重要——作为创始人，了解需要完成的工作以洞察卓越表现的标准真的很重要。对我们来说，当时的生态系统中经验丰富的人才供应相对匮乏。所以对我来说，很难说"哦，让我们从Y组织聘请具备Z职位描述的X人"，因为我们知道他们很可能无法胜任这份工作——毕竟人才资源实在太少了。（00:41:16）所以很多时候我不得不去理解：好吧，这个职位到底是做什么的？具体职责是什么？看看自己在这方面做得有多糟糕，才能明白优秀的标准是什么。因此，我承担了许多这些角色，就是为了尽可能深入了解业务的每个环节，进而找到能比我强出几个数量级的人才。除了司机这个角色，我对其他所有职位都是如此。作为司机，我并不想去理解司机的卓越表现是什么。显然，司机们的工作极具挑战性，我只想了解他们的工作内容，从而对他们的需求有更深的同理心，并确保我们的产品能满足这些需求。（00:42:12）所以当我们首次推出网约车服务时，我记得自己是应用上首位真正的司机，偶尔也会开车接单。记得早期有一次接单，一位女士把目的地设为商场。我开车到了她家楼下，发现她拿了一个巨型行李袋，要我帮她把行李放进后备箱，然后继续接送客人。中途她又说"我去商场前还要顺便洗衣服"。我只能说"好吧，不错"。于是我们绕路送她去商场，但这次经历几乎没赚到钱，也没即时反馈。但这最终促使我为司机团队提供支持，当他们提出"我们需要提高等候费，增加中途停靠点以补偿额外工作量"时，我深有共鸣。这都是我亲身经历过的，也是我为开发司机应用时所推崇的一系列产品特性和原则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like having to do that ends up being a feature as you said, that you actually experienced a lot of these challenges and you said the really good point about knowing what to hire and what these people are going to actually do.
turns.zh: 看起来你不得不亲自做这些事，最终成了一个特色功能，正如你所说，自己经历过很多挑战，也对招聘标准和司机实际工作有了深刻理解。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's interesting how that often turns into a good thing. I know you also have a pretty interesting journey into tech. What can you share around that?
turns.zh: 真有趣的是，这事儿往往能转化成好事。我知道你自己在科技领域的经历也相当精彩，能跟我们分享一下吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: So I am basically a failed finance professional. I didn't really know what I wanted to do in my life. And in 2005, which is when I entered college, the hot sexy thing to do was finance. And I guess that was what I wanted to do. And I went, studied finance, and then the crash of 2008 happened and I graduated 2009, so it's probably the worst time to try and be a finance professional. And so I went through a really challenging time there, but eventually I got a job at a boutique investment banking firm. And that was, I thought like, okay, now I was set for life. I got the job that I wanted. I'm working in finance. But then long story short, I was not very good. I was not very good. My bosses thought I was underperforming. I didn't feel like I was performing, and I kind of left that field that I thought I built my entire, I guess future dreams and identity around. (00:45:32): And after I did that, I decided to take a bet in Indonesian technology because when all of this was happening was around 2010, 2011, and it was starting to see the development of the current technology giants in the US at the time. And I thought that it would be pretty cool if Indonesia ever had a technology industry to be part of it at the ground floor. And so I moved back in 2011 and it was super early. It was really early at the time where the level of talent, the level of funding, the level of product market fit, the number of people who transacted on the internet was also still super low. People still saw the internet as a place for chat apps and social media. And so the level of belief that people had in the space at that time was pretty low. (00:46:30): People didn't think that real businesses and real valuable products could be built, especially be built locally. And so taking that bet was something that I think it really panned out for us to be really early in the space, which today has become very vibrant to the scene. Southeast Asia has become, I think one of the most exciting spaces in technology in the world to date. But at the time it wasn't obvious. And being able to see that development I think was something that was really important to me because it really shows you what's possible in a very short time. And I think it's something that probably people in technology in the US can relate to, the people who've been working in this space for like 20, 30 years. But being able to see those early days for me was just really valuable and I think was an experience that I definitely cherish.
turns.zh: 所以说，我基本上算是个失败的金融从业者。我当时完全不知道自己想干什么。2005年上大学的时候，金融行业可是最热门的选择。我觉得那就是我想从事的行业。于是我去学了金融，后来2008年金融危机爆发，我2009年毕业，那时候想成为金融从业者简直是最糟糕的时机了。所以我经历了一段非常艰难的时期，但最终在一家精品投行找到了工作。当时我还想，嗯，我的人生算是稳了。我得到了梦寐以求的工作，终于进入了金融行业。但长话短说，我表现不佳。我的上司觉得我业绩不达标，我自己也觉得做得不好。于是我离开了这个我曾以为会为之奉献未来、构建身份认同的行业。（00:45:32）之后，2010年、2011年左右，印尼科技行业开始发展，而当时美国的科技巨头也正崭露头角。我当时想，如果印尼能拥有自己的科技产业，那该多酷啊！于是2011年我回国，那时候还太早了。当时的人才储备、资金水平、产品与市场的契合度都很低，互联网用户数量也很少。人们还把互联网当作聊天应用和社交媒体的平台，对这个领域的信心非常低。（00:46:30）人们不相信能在这里诞生真正的商业和有价值的产品，尤其是本土化的。但我们在早期押注这个领域，后来证明这是个正确的选择，如今这个领域已经非常活跃。东南亚已经成为全球最令人兴奋的科技生态之一。但当时这一切并不显而易见。亲眼见证这个发展过程对我来说意义非凡，它让我看到短时间内就能创造奇迹的可能性。这或许也是美国科技从业者能感同身受的，那些在这一行深耕二三十年的人。但对我来说，见证早期阶段的价值无与伦比，我认为这段经历值得珍视。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's really hard to just build a company outside of Silicon Valley, and it was even harder back then. COVID and remote work almost made it the easiest it's ever been.
turns.zh: 在硅谷以外创办公司确实很难，当时更是难上加难。新冠疫情和远程办公几乎让这件事变得前所未有的容易。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like a lot of the fact that you were so far away from the Bay Area informed the way that you built this company, the scrappiness that you talked about. I'm curious if you have any advice for a founder who's trying to build a company now outside of, say the Bay Area or just US in general based on your experience.
turns.zh: 看来你远离湾区这件事对公司建设方式产生了很大影响，也让你提到了你所说的灵活应变精神。我很好奇，根据你的经验，你对那些想在湾区以外、甚至整个美国以外创办公司的创始人有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yeah, look, it was super hard back then. It was particularly hard because Indonesia is such a valuable market, Indonesia and the rest, I would say primarily Indonesia just because of its scale. But I think overall Southeast Asia was just such a valuable market and it was interesting for global companies to want to win it. So we competed with global and regional companies, but the local talent and funding ecosystems were really underdeveloped. So that challenge of having to compete with the best in the world for customers in the market while also not having all of the resources available within the market to be able to build products and companies that can compete was I would say one of the most challenging parts of building probably in markets that are atypical or outside of Silicon Valley and maybe some of the other technology centers in the world like China and India. (00:49:01): So some of my learnings probably there that I would take going forward is I think we talked a lot about being scrappy. In the beginning, we were a lot more ops-heavy than tech-heavy. And doing the things that don't scale through other means I think is definitely something that is absolutely necessary if you're building outside of these main technology hubs. Another thing I would say is you need to get good at remote work really early. And I think today that's kind of become a lot more prevalent as more and more people have experience with remote work. For us, we built an engineering center in Bangalore in 2015, and this allowed us to compete a lot better with the global giants because we had access to a really deep talent market in India at the time, but we were really early in this whole remote work thing because it wasn't common for people in our region, but also globally to have so much talent concentration outside of headquarters. (00:50:14): And I do believe that companies who want to compete against world class competitors outside of these technology centers like Silicon Valley need to become good at remote work really fast because getting that talent probably means having offices or individuals who are outside of your home market or your headquarters. And probably the final I would say tip here is don't just copy, because Gojek was not an Uber clone, even though that was kind of how some investors or analysts talk about us, we were focused on a solution that was uniquely an Indonesian phenomenon, the motorcycle taxi driver. And this led to both product and branding innovation. On the product side, we were an on-demand super app because we saw that a human being on a motorcycle could do a lot of things. And so we built a product around that idea and hence we ended up with a super app even before super apps were really a thing. (00:51:24): And then that branding point that we talked about a little earlier about giving our drivers jackets and helmets so people could see them zip around town, which actually doesn't make sense if you're a car ride hailing service because it's not very easy to brand a car and the drivers are inside the car. But all of our competitors at the time when they first entered the motorcycle ride hailing space didn't brand their drivers because they came from a car-centric view. And so again, understanding your unique market dynamics is also really important if you're building outside of these technology centers.
turns.zh:
是啊，你看，当时确实非常困难。特别困难的原因在于印度尼西亚是一个极具价值的市场——尤其是印度尼西亚，我会说主要是因为它的市场规模。但我认为总体而言，东南亚是一个极具价值的市场，全球公司都渴望在这里胜出。因此，我们与全球和地区性公司竞争，但当地的人才和融资生态系统确实不发达。在市场上与世界顶尖公司争夺客户的同时，又缺乏本地资源来打造具有竞争力的产品和公司，这种挑战可以说是，在硅谷等传统科技中心之外，以及中国、印度等其他科技中心之外，建设业务最具挑战性的部分之一。

（00:49:01）：所以我从中吸取的经验教训是，我们经常谈到要灵活应变。最初，我们更侧重于运营而非技术。通过其他手段无法扩展的业务，我认为这对在这些主要科技中心以外地区创业的公司来说绝对是必要的。另外，我想说的是，你需要尽早擅长远程工作。如今，随着越来越多人拥有远程工作经验，这已变得越来越普遍。2015年，我们在班加罗尔建立了一个工程中心，这使我们能更好地与全球巨头竞争，因为当时印度拥有深厚的技术人才储备。但我们很早就开始尝试远程工作，因为在我们所在的地区乃至全球，人才集中于总部以外的情况并不常见。

（00:50:14）：我坚信，想要在硅谷等科技中心以外与世界级竞争对手抗衡的公司，必须迅速掌握远程工作技能，因为获取这些人才可能意味着要在本土市场或总部以外设立办事处或招募人才。最后我想说的是，不要简单地抄袭。Gojek并非Uber的克隆版，尽管有些投资者或分析师这样说，但我们专注于解决印度尼西亚特有的问题——摩托车出租车司机。这促成了产品和品牌创新。在产品层面，我们打造了一款按需超级应用，因为我们发现骑摩托车的人能做很多事情。基于这一理念，我们开发了产品，最终在超级应用概念流行之前就打造了超级应用。关于品牌建设，我们提到过给司机发放夹克和头盔，让人们能看到他们在城市中穿梭。这在汽车网约车服务中其实没意义，因为汽车很难品牌化，而且司机在车内。但当时所有进入摩托车网约车领域的竞争对手都忽视了司机的品牌化，因为他们来自以汽车为核心的视角。因此，理解独特的市场动态在科技中心以外地区创业时也至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've been chatting about Indonesia and Southeast Asia. I'd love to hear just what should people know about that market? We've chatted about what you guys have built and a few other companies here and there, but what companies should people be aware of what's happening? What's the latest, what's exciting?
turns.zh: 我们一直在聊印度尼西亚和东南亚。我很想听听大家对这个市场的了解都有哪些？我们之前讨论了你们公司以及其他一些零星提到的公司，但还有哪些公司值得关注？最新的动态是什么？哪些事态最令人兴奋？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yeah, I think specifically Indonesia, most people don't know that Indonesia is the fourth largest country in the world and that Southeast Asia holds almost 10% of the world's population. But beyond the macro picture, I think also we've experienced a pretty unique level of pace of adoption for products with great product market fit. So products with great product market fit grow tremendously fast in this part of the world. And in 2015, for example, when we launched our app, we grew more than a hundred percent month on month for the first 16, 18 months. So we more than doubled every month for more than a year.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得具体说到印度尼西亚，大多数人都不知道印度尼西亚是世界第四大国，而且东南亚地区的人口占全球总人口的近10%。但除了宏观层面，我认为我们还见证了产品与市场高度契合的案例在该地区的惊人增长速度。在这里，这种产品与市场高度契合的模式能让产品快速扩张。例如，2015年我们推出应用时，前16、18个月每月用户增长超100%，一年多来每月用户数翻倍不止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is insane. I've never heard of that.
turns.zh: 这太不可思议了。我从未听说过这样的情况。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: No, and our investors at the time, Sequoia is one of our investors at the time, told us that this was the craziest growth story that they've ever heard of in the world. And I wouldn't say because of our necessarily our brilliance, it was a combination of how in Indonesia and in Southeast Asia, there are a lot of these things that are obviously broken and could be improved with better technology and better products. But we also have in this region a very young population who are excited to try new things. And so if you find a solution that really resonates with a lot of these common day-to-day problems, the adoption curve is just absolutely insane. And I think it's one of the things that are definitely unique to developing regions like this one. (00:54:14): One company that's really interesting for example, just to give a flavor of the type of seemingly off the wall product or company being built in this part of the world, there's a company called eFishery, and what they do is they basically create a closed loop ecosystem for fish farmers in currently, I think they're only operational Indonesia or they're recently expanding beyond Indonesia. (00:54:45): They help farmers feed their fish through this IOT smart device that helps measure the amount of fish feed that needs to go into the ponds, but they also then help farmers do things that get financing and also sell their produce out to local or even regional or global markets. And it's a company doing something like a quarter billion dollars in revenue and it's profitable and it's basically a fish farmer, a close loop ecosystem. And it's pretty wild that something like this exists, but it does speak to, I think again earlier what I said earlier about the hunger that the population have for better solutions. And if you can find these better solutions, you can really build companies of the very meaningful scale very, very quickly.
turns.zh:
没错。当时我们的投资方红杉资本告诉我们，这是他们在全球见过增长最快的案例。倒不是因为我们有多高明，而是因为印尼和东南亚地区存在诸多明显有待改进的痛点，比如技术和产品能带来显著提升。此外，这里的人口年轻，对新事物充满热情。因此，如果能找到真正能解决日常问题的解决方案，用户增长速度会快得令人惊叹。这也是发展中地区独有的优势。
（00:54:14）：举个有趣的例子，比如eFishery公司。他们为养鱼户打造了一个闭环生态系统，目前主要在印尼运营，最近也在向其他国家扩张。通过物联网智能设备，他们帮助养鱼户精准投放饲料，还能帮助养鱼户获取融资，并将产品销售至本地、区域乃至全球市场。该公司年营收达25亿美元，且实现盈利，堪称养鱼户的闭环生态系统。这样的创新令人惊叹，也印证了我之前提到的当地民众对优质解决方案的迫切需求。只要能找到这样的解决方案，就能迅速打造出极具影响力的企业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So at this point, you've stepped down a CEO, you've stepped down from the board, what's next and how does it feel?
turns.zh: 那你卸任CEO和董事会职务后，接下来有什么计划？感受如何？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yeah, I'm still on this journey honestly, of how does it feel. I think that building Gojek is by far the most important professional experience and frankly, one of the most important life experiences I've had. It's made me a way better person actually. And now that I've stepped away, I am not as bored or as aimless as people would expect after having such a kind of all-consuming thing be part of my life experience. (00:56:37): What's next? Honestly, Lenny, I don't know. I don't have a plan at this stage. I do some angel investing on the side. I work with other founders to be able to maybe just share some of these experiences that I shared today and just figuring out what makes me happy and what are the kind activities that I find rewarding. I don't know, maybe I'll start another company at some point. I think that's my default, but I think right now I'm just taking things easy and trying to figure out another problem I guess, that I could be obsessed about.
turns.zh: 是啊，说实话，我现在仍在探索这段旅程，感受它是怎样的体验。我觉得创立Gojek是迄今为止最重要的职业经历，坦白说，也是我人生中最重要的经历之一。它让我成为了一个更好的人。如今退出后，人们可能觉得我会变得无聊或迷茫，但事实并非如此。毕竟，这样一种全身心投入的事物曾占据我的生活经历，我并不感到空虚或迷茫。（00:56:37）接下来会怎样？说实话，莱尼，我也不确定。目前我没有明确的计划。我偶尔会做些天使投资，帮助其他创业者，或许能把今天分享的这些经验传授给他们，同时也在探索什么能让我快乐，什么样的活动能给我带来满足感。说不定哪天我会再创办一家公司呢。这或许是我的默认选择，但目前我只想放慢脚步，尝试破解下一个让我沉迷其中的难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've earned that time to explore and look for new problems. Is there anything else you wanted to touch on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 你完全有时间去探索和寻找新的挑战。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: No Lenny. I think we've covered a lot today, and I just wanted to thank you for the time.
turns.zh: 没有了，莱尼。我觉得今天已经聊了很多，我只想感谢你的时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. It's absolutely my pleasure. And with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这完全是我的荣幸。接下来就是激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我准备了五个问题，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yes, let's go.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: What You Do Is Who You Are. I think that was the second most popular Ben Horowitz's book, but I'm really obsessed with building interesting and engaging cultures, so I think that's one. Another is a classic marketing book. Again, we talked a lot about branding today, so there's this book called How Brands Grow by Byron Sharp. I don't agree necessarily with everything in it, but I do think that it's a great primer on how to think about branding and marketing.
turns.zh: 《你所做即你所是》。我觉得这是本·霍洛维茨第二受欢迎的书，但我对打造有趣且吸引人的企业文化很着迷，所以这本书是首选。另一本是经典营销书籍。今天我们聊了很多品牌建设，所以有本叫《品牌如何成长》的书。虽说我不完全认同书中的所有观点，但我认为它是理解品牌和营销的绝佳入门读物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Favorite recent movie, The Menu and favorite recent TV show? Netflix show is a Cyberpunk 2077 Edge Runners.
turns.zh: 最近最喜欢的电影是《菜单》，电视剧是网飞的《赛博朋克2077：边缘行者》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow. I haven't heard of that one.
turns.zh: 哇，我还没听说过这部。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Oh, you should check it out. It's super cool.
turns.zh: 你真该看看，超酷的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'll go check it out.
turns.zh: 我去看看。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite interview question that you like to ask.
turns.zh: 你最喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Tell me about a subject or activity you've been obsessed with for a long time.
turns.zh: 谈谈你长期痴迷的某个主题或活动吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you look for in an answer that's like, okay, this is good.
turns.zh: 你如何判断一个回答是否合格？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: I want somebody to basically almost pitch to me an obsession they have than makes me interested in knowing more into that subject. The more obscure, the better and the more passionate they are about an obscure thing, even better. And I think it shows people's capability to be really passionate about something and sell something and think about something in a very structured and detailed way.
turns.zh: 我希望对方能基本向我推销他们的痴迷，让我对那个主题产生兴趣。越冷门越好，他们对冷门事物越有热情，就越棒。我觉得这能展示出人们对某件事充满热情、善于推销并能以结构化和细致的方式思考问题的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some products that you love and have recently discovered?
turns.zh: 最近有没有发现什么让你爱不释手的产品？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Two products, I think right now that I've found absolutely delightful. One is the ARC Browser. I know that it's gaining a lot of traction out there, but I'm a very chronic tab hoarder. My Chrome tabs are just all over the place, and I love that they've figured out I would say the best approach to kind of tab management, and there's just a ton of little delightful, awesome design details in the app that I think is just really cool. And it's a browser. When's the last time there was a really cool browser that came out? So I also love the ambition that the company has. (01:00:09): Second product, Steam Deck. I'm a huge gamer, and I think it is probably, I would say the best game platform to actually build on the vision of truly portable mobile gaming.
turns.zh: 有两个产品，我觉得现在发现的特别棒。一个是ARC浏览器。我知道它现在很受欢迎，但我一直是个超级标签控。我的Chrome标签页乱七八糟的，而他们想出了我认为是管理标签页最有效的方法，应用里还有很多可爱又实用的小设计细节，真的很棒。毕竟浏览器这种产品多久才出一个特别酷的了？所以我也欣赏这家公司的雄心壮志。（01:00:09）第二个产品是Steam Deck。我是个游戏爱好者，我觉得它可能是真正实现便携移动游戏愿景的最佳平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love your point with ARC for tab hoarders. I also used to have a lot of tabs and I love it just auto deletes stuff and just disappear, and it forces you to lose your tabs and it works out surprisingly.
turns.zh: 我很赞同你关于ARC对标签控的看法。我以前也常有太多标签页，现在它能自动删除或隐藏标签，倒逼你清理标签页，效果出奇地好。

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: Final question.
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious what comes up for this one? What's something you've recently changed or that you've heard of someone at Gojek recently changed in their product development process that was maybe minor, that had a tremendous impact on the team's ability to execute.
turns.zh: 我很好奇大家会想到什么？你最近在Gojek的产品开发流程中做过什么改变，或者听说谁做过什么小改进，但却对团队执行能力产生了巨大影响？

turns.speaker: Kevin Aluwi
turns.en: One relatively minor thing that I thought had a lot of impact with execution is being very clear that whoever is accountable for the results should also be the decider. I found that a lot of literature out there says that product teams should be this communal best ideas come from everywhere group, which I think is well-intentioned and absolutely everyone should contribute ideas, but I think not having it be super clear who is accountable and who is deciding often slows down execution a lot. And I think when we switch to making it really clear that who was the decider for any kind of product development process, I think our execution definitely improved significantly.
